title: Former White House AI Advisors: Chip Restrictions Aren't About Suppressing China, They're About Buying Time for Safety
dek: Two former White House AI advisors say chip restrictions on China aren't meant to contain its rise, but to trade computing advantage for time to solve AI safety—yet China's opening move in Geneva talks was just one sentence: ‘sell us chips first’.
why: Hear from the two officials who shaped China chip policy explain how hard-line restrictions and openness to dialogue—even urging restraint—fit together in their view.
who: Policy researchers, tech journalists and investors tracking US-China AI competition, export control policy, and the direction of AI regulation.
skip: Around the 19-minute mark, banter about ‘making it into a movie’ can be skipped without losing the thread of the argument.

points.h: GPT-3 proved scale laws in a way papers could not
points.body: Ben Buchanan says his faith in scale laws wasn't immediate. He'd read Dario Amodei's memo on ‘compute at scale’and Rich Sutton's 2019 article The Bitter Lesson, but GPT-3's release in May 2020 was what truly convinced him. That conviction led him to write in Foreign Affairs that compute would become central to national security—a chain of reasoning that pulled in a small group pushing for China chip export restrictions.

points.h: Skeptics of determinism become true believers in individual power
points.body: Buchanan entered government believing scale laws would necessarily come true. He left certain that ‘individual impact was astonishing’—not just the initial handful who believed in this, but also people like Jake Sullivan and Bruce Reed who would listen to them. Without those individuals, he thinks the history of China chip restrictions might look completely different.

points.h: Hundred-to-one computing lead, held back by political will
points.body: Buchanan offers numbers: even with Trump administration enforcement failures and partial openings, the US and allies hold about 100:1 advantage in computing production over China, and 15:1 in computing access. Closing off remote access and transshipment loopholes could widen both. But the real constraint over the past 1-2 years wasn't capability—it was ‘belief that this technology truly matters’. David Sacks' push to ‘let the private sector handle it’and JD Vance's mocking of safety in his Paris speech have both slowed the work of spending the lead on safety.

points.h: At Geneva, China's opening move was: ‘sell us the chips’
points.body: Nathan proposes treating AI itself—not China—as the true ‘alien’, and suggests ‘trading chips for oversight’ to unlock cooperation. Buchanan pushes back: would you really make GPU sales the precondition for talks? He recalls that in Geneva talks in May 2024, China's opening position was simply ‘sell us chips, and we can discuss other things later’. Unless he sees real movement, he won't surrender the ‘leverage point’ of computing advantage.

points.h: Ban closed-loop AI self-improvement; use railroad-era safety as the model
points.body: Buchanan cites the 1870s railroad industry, where unified brakes, couplers, and gauge made the industry both safer and faster. He advocates mandatory pre-deployment testing of AI systems, resident government evaluators, and government control of the pacing. If forced to choose one ‘blunt tool’ regulation, he'd ban closed-loop recursive self-improvement rather than impose date-based pauses—because pausing for the sake of pausing just creates compute overhang, and when pauses lift, capability surges discontinuously rather than resuming gradually.

points.h: AI became a major voting issue: 56% say it shaped their choice
points.body: Buchanan says 2026 was the first time AI became a central election issue. Fifty-six percent of voters said it was key or important to their vote. He expects AI to be the top issue by 2028, tangled up with cost of living and corruption. Asked about claims that data-center referendums are Chinese influence operations, he flatly denies it: Americans worry about AI because Americans are worrying about AI.

points.h: Democratic oversight through elections can't keep pace with AI-enabled government power
points.body: Tantum Collins raises the ‘bitter temptation’: even if we solve safety correctly, navigate global governance rightly, and maintain our computing lead, AI could grant governments vastly more concentrated power—while the public's ability to oversee them stays static. Collins compares elections to ‘low-information, low-frequency multiple choice forms’—a terrible information-RL environment for accountability. The antidote is letting ‘popular sovereignty’ scale up with government capability.

points.h: The world learned of AI's cyber-weapons because Anthropic gave them to defenders first
points.body: Buchanan expects the first real AI emergency to come from cyber or biological domains—perhaps North Korea attacking banks, or a jailbreak like the Hugging Face incident evolving into a persistent agent swarm. The public knows how capable AI is at cyber offense only because Anthropic and OpenAI this year shared those capabilities with the defending side—government security partners. Buchanan would bet his entire fortune that if China had equivalent capabilities first, they would use them against US infrastructure, not disclose them. The fact that we know what's possible reflects a choice about whose side disclosure serves.
